note:
Doctor: Come on in. Your intake says you're a 30-year-old female, back from a long trip, and you brought a CT report with you. Tell me what's going on.
Patient: Yeah, I got back five days ago from three weeks in Southeast Asia. About a week into the trip I had really bad watery diarrhea and belly cramps, so I went to a private hospital there and they did a CT scan of my abdomen. They said the cramps were from an infection, but there was a spot on my left adrenal gland, 2.3 centimeters, and I should get it checked when I got home.
Doctor: Okay, let me read it. It says a well-defined left adrenal nodule, 2.3 centimeters, low density at about 8 Hounsfield units, no calcification, nothing else abnormal. That pattern is reassuring and looks like a benign adenoma, but we still have to check whether it's making hormones. How is the diarrhea now?
Patient: Mostly better. I still have loose stools, maybe twice a day, and some cramping. They gave me azithromycin 500 mg once daily for three days and I finished it. I've also been taking loperamide 2 mg when I need it, and ibuprofen 400 mg for the cramps.
Doctor: Any fever or blood in the stool?
Patient: No fever, and no blood.
Doctor: Now the adrenal questions. Any spells of pounding heart, sweating, or headaches?
Patient: No, nothing like that. No palpitations and no headaches.
Doctor: Easy bruising, weight gain around the middle, or muscle weakness?
Patient: No, none of that. My weight has been steady, I actually lost a couple of pounds on the trip.
Doctor: Do you take anything else?
Patient: Just my birth control pill.
Doctor: Good to know, because the estrogen in it can throw off one of the cortisol tests, so we will account for that. Your blood pressure today is 134/84, heart rate 78, temperature 98.6, oxygen saturation 99 percent, and the fingerstick glucose is 92. Your abdomen is soft with mild diffuse tenderness, no guarding, and I don't see any bruising or stretch marks.
Patient: So what does this mean?
Doctor: My impression is an adrenal incidentaloma, probably a benign adenoma, plus traveler's diarrhea that is improving. Here is the plan. I'll order plasma metanephrines, a 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test, an aldosterone and renin level, and a basic metabolic panel. Stop the loperamide since your stools are nearly normal. Stop the ibuprofen and use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed instead. Drink plenty of fluids. I'll also refer you to our endocrinology clinic so they can decide about repeat imaging. Come back sooner if you get fever, bloody stool, or severe headaches with sweating.
Patient: Okay, that sounds good.
summary: A 30-year-old female came to urgent care after three weeks of international travel with a CT report from an overseas hospital showing a 2.3 centimeter left adrenal nodule found during evaluation of watery diarrhea and cramps. The diarrhea is improving, and she denies fever, blood in the stool, palpitations, headaches, easy bruising, weight gain and muscle weakness. Vitals were stable with a fingerstick glucose of 92, and the abdomen had mild diffuse tenderness. The clinician assessed an adrenal incidentaloma, probably a benign adenoma, plus improving traveler's diarrhea. Plan includes plasma metanephrines, a dexamethasone suppression test, aldosterone and renin levels, a basic metabolic panel, stopping loperamide and ibuprofen, acetaminophen as needed, and endocrinology referral.

Blood pressure 134/84, heart rate 78, temperature 98.6, oxygen saturation 99 percent, fingerstick glucose 92. Abdomen soft with mild diffuse tenderness and no guarding; no bruising or stretch marks.

plan: Order plasma metanephrines
Order a 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test, accounting for the estrogen in her birth control pill
Order an aldosterone and renin level
Order a basic metabolic panel

note:
Telehealth visit conducted by synchronous video, with the patient at home and the clinician in clinic. A professional Spanish medical interpreter joined the video call for the entire visit, and the patient gave verbal consent for telehealth. This is a 73-year-old male followed for stable exertional angina.

Reason for visit: routine follow-up of exertional chest pressure.

History from the patient through the interpreter: Chest pressure comes on when he walks uphill or climbs two flights of stairs, lasts 3 to 5 minutes, and goes away with rest. It has happened about twice a week for the past 2 months with no change in pattern. He used sublingual nitroglycerin 0.4 mg twice in the past month with relief within a few minutes. He denies chest pain at rest, denies pain that wakes him from sleep, denies palpitations, denies syncope or lightheadedness, and denies orthopnea or leg swelling. He reports mild shortness of breath only at the same level of exertion that brings on the chest pressure. Past history includes CAD with a stent placed 6 years ago, HTN, T2DM, and hyperlipidemia. He has no known drug allergies.

Medication reconciliation: He first stated that he takes metoprolol succinate 100 mg once daily. When asked to hold the bottle up to the camera, the label read 50 mg once daily; correction, he has been taking metoprolol succinate 50 mg once daily, not 100 mg. His other medications are aspirin 81 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, lisinopril 20 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, and sublingual nitroglycerin 0.4 mg as needed. He also takes over-the-counter supplements: fish oil 1000 mg daily, garlic capsules, and ginkgo biloba, which he started 3 months ago for memory.

Home measurements: BP 138/82 and 134/80 on repeat with his home cuff, pulse 64, and 97% on his home pulse oximeter.

Video examination: He appears comfortable and speaks in full sentences with no respiratory distress, and his gait across the room is steady. There is no visible lower extremity edema when he showed his ankles to the camera. Heart and lung auscultation could not be performed by video.

Recent data: Labs 3 weeks ago showed LDL 68 mg/dL, A1c 7.2%, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, and potassium 4.4. The exercise stress test 4 weeks ago reached 7 METs, was stopped for leg fatigue, and showed 1.5 mm of ST depression in the lateral leads at peak exercise that resolved in recovery, with no arrhythmia. The echocardiogram showed an ejection fraction of 58% with no significant valve disease.

Impression: Stable exertional angina, Canadian Cardiovascular Society class II, on a lower beta-blocker dose than he believed, with home blood pressure above goal. T2DM and hyperlipidemia are reasonably controlled. His ginkgo biloba adds bleeding risk on top of aspirin.

Management: Increase metoprolol succinate from 50 mg to 100 mg once daily. Stop ginkgo biloba because of the bleeding risk with aspirin; he may continue fish oil, and I asked him to read me the label of every supplement at the next visit. Continue aspirin 81 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, lisinopril 20 mg daily, and metformin 1000 mg twice daily. Refilled sublingual nitroglycerin 0.4 mg; reviewed taking one tablet at the onset of pain and calling emergency services if the pain is not gone 5 minutes after the first dose. He should call the clinic if his pulse falls below 50 or he becomes dizzy. Order an ECG at an in-person visit and a basic metabolic panel in 4 weeks. Teach-back was completed through the interpreter. Follow up by video in 4 weeks with a home BP and pulse log.
summary: A 73-year-old male with CAD, HTN, T2DM and hyperlipidemia had a telehealth video visit, with a professional Spanish interpreter, for follow-up of stable exertional angina. Chest pressure occurs with uphill walking or two flights of stairs about twice a week and resolves with rest, and he denies rest pain, palpitations, syncope and leg swelling. After checking the bottle he clarified that he takes metoprolol succinate 50 mg once daily, not 100 mg, and he also uses fish oil, garlic capsules and ginkgo biloba. Stress testing showed lateral ST depression at peak exercise. Metoprolol succinate is increased to 100 mg once daily and ginkgo biloba is stopped for bleeding risk, with an ECG and basic metabolic panel planned.

Echocardiogram showed an ejection fraction of 58% with no significant valve disease.

Video follow-up in 4 weeks with a home BP and pulse log

note:
Hospital day 2 for this 58-year-old male admitted with acute urinary retention due to benign prostatic hyperplasia with lower urinary tract symptoms. He presented with inability to void for 12 hours and lower abdominal pain, on top of several months of weak stream, hesitancy, and nocturia 3 to 4 times nightly. A bladder scan on arrival showed more than 900 mL, and a Foley catheter was placed with 950 mL of clear yellow urine drained. The retention was likely precipitated by an over-the-counter cold remedy containing a decongestant that he took for 2 days before arrival. He denies fever, dysuria, hematuria, and flank pain. Overnight he had no complaints, and the catheter has drained clear urine with good output.

Before admission he was taking no prescription medications. For urinary symptoms he has been using saw palmetto 320 mg daily and a zinc supplement 30 mg daily, both purchased over the counter. In hospital he was started on tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily on admission, and finasteride 5 mg daily was added today. He has needed acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for suprapubic discomfort only once.

Vitals this morning: BP 138/84, HR 76, temperature 98.2 F, RR 16, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. On exam he is comfortable, the abdomen is soft with no suprapubic tenderness now, and there is no costovertebral angle tenderness. Digital rectal exam shows a smooth, symmetrically enlarged prostate, estimated at about 50 grams, without nodules or tenderness.

Data: Creatinine was 1.5 on admission and is 1.1 today. Urinalysis was negative for nitrite and leukocyte esterase, and the urine culture shows no growth so far. PSA is 3.8, drawn before finasteride was started. Renal ultrasound showed mild bilateral hydronephrosis that is expected to improve with decompression.

Impression is benign prostatic hyperplasia with lower urinary tract symptoms, complicated by acute urinary retention that is now decompressed, with a mild obstructive rise in creatinine that is resolving.

Plan: Keep the Foley catheter overnight and continue tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily. Continue the new finasteride 5 mg daily. Perform a trial without catheter tomorrow morning after at least 48 hours of tamsulosin, with a bladder scan for post-void residual after he voids. Stop saw palmetto and the zinc supplement, since they have not been shown to help BPH, and he agreed. He was counseled to avoid decongestant and antihistamine cold remedies and to check labels. Repeat creatinine tomorrow. Urology clinic follow-up in 2 weeks. If he fails the trial, he will go home with a catheter and further evaluation will be arranged.
summary: A 58-year-old male was admitted with acute urinary retention from benign prostatic hyperplasia with lower urinary tract symptoms, likely precipitated by an over-the-counter decongestant cold remedy. On hospital day 2 the Foley catheter is draining clear urine, creatinine has improved from 1.5 to 1.1, urinalysis and culture are unremarkable, and the exam shows a smooth, enlarged prostate. He denies fever, dysuria, hematuria and flank pain, and he had been using saw palmetto and a zinc supplement. Tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily continues and finasteride 5 mg daily is added. Saw palmetto and zinc are stopped, a trial without catheter is planned for tomorrow, and urology follow-up is arranged in 2 weeks.

note:
Telehealth video visit for neurology follow-up. The patient is a 38-year-old male who connected from home with good audio and video quality and gave verbal consent for the visit.

He reports a 3-year history of shaking in both hands that has slowly worsened. The tremor appears when he holds a cup of coffee, writes, or uses a spoon, and it improves when his hands are resting in his lap. Stress and caffeine make it worse. His father had a similar hand tremor. He denies tremor at rest, stiffness, slowness of movement, numbness, weakness, and falls. He takes no regular medications and has no other medical conditions.

Home vitals measured with his own cuff: blood pressure 122/76 and pulse 72.

On video examination he is alert and speaks clearly. With his arms outstretched there is a fine, symmetric postural tremor of both hands that increases slightly when he reaches for his nose. He drew a spiral on paper held up to the camera and the line was wavy. There is no tremor at rest while seated, no head tremor, his facial expression is normal, and his arm swing is normal as he walks across the room.

Impression is essential tremor, with no features of Parkinson disease. Plan is to start propranolol 20 mg twice daily and to cut back to one cup of coffee a day. I ordered a TSH to exclude a thyroid cause. He has no asthma, so a beta-blocker is appropriate, and he was told to call if his pulse falls below 55 or he feels dizzy. Follow up by video in 6 weeks.
summary: A 38-year-old male had a neurology telehealth video visit for a 3-year history of slowly worsening bilateral hand shaking that appears with holding a cup, writing or using a spoon. He denies tremor at rest, stiffness, slowness of movement, numbness, weakness and falls, takes no regular medications, and has a similar tremor in his father. Video examination showed a fine symmetric postural tremor and a wavy spiral drawing without rest or head tremor. The impression is essential tremor, and the plan is to start propranolol 20 mg twice daily, limit coffee, order a TSH, and follow up by video in 6 weeks.

This is a 25-year-old female, G1P0 at 36 weeks of pregnancy, admitted from triage for evaluation of elevated blood pressure found at her routine prenatal visit. She reports mild swelling in her feet for the past week. She denies headache, visual changes, right upper quadrant pain, vaginal bleeding, and leakage of fluid, and she reports normal fetal movement. She has no chronic medical conditions and takes only a prenatal vitamin once daily.

On arrival her blood pressure was 148/94, and it was 152/98 when repeated 4 hours later. Heart rate is 82, temperature 98.4 F, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. She is comfortable. Examination shows trace pedal edema, a nontender abdomen, and brisk but normal reflexes without clonus. The fetal heart rate is 140 beats per minute with a reactive non-stress test and no decelerations.

Labs show platelets 214, creatinine 0.7, and normal liver enzymes. The urine protein to creatinine ratio is 0.52.

Impression is preeclampsia without severe features at 36 weeks. Plan is to continue admission for observation with blood pressure checks every 4 hours and fetal monitoring, to start labetalol 200 mg twice daily, to continue the prenatal vitamin once daily, to repeat the CBC, creatinine, and liver enzymes tomorrow, and to plan induction of labor at 37 weeks. She was counseled to report headache, visual changes, or upper abdominal pain right away.

The impression is preeclampsia without severe features. Plan is observation with fetal monitoring, labetalol 200 mg twice daily, repeat labs tomorrow, and induction of labor at 37 weeks.

note:
Doctor: Hello, I'm the emergency doctor. I see you're a 60-year-old male with diabetes, and the nurse says you've been feeling terrible. What's been going on?
Patient: I've been sick for about three days. I caught some stomach bug and I was throwing up, couldn't keep anything down, so I stopped taking my insulin because I wasn't eating. Now I'm so thirsty I can't stop drinking, I'm peeing all the time, and my stomach hurts.
Doctor: Which insulin do you take, and how much?
Patient: Lantus, insulin glargine, 30 units at night. And I take metformin 1000 mg twice a day.
Doctor: And how many nights did you skip the glargine?
Patient: Three. Wait, no, it was two nights. I took it the first night I got sick and then I stopped.
Doctor: Got it, two nights. Any fever, chest pain, or cough?
Patient: No fever, no chest pain, no cough. No diarrhea either, just the vomiting. I do feel weak and my breathing feels fast, like I can't catch my breath.
Doctor: Okay. Your vitals are blood pressure 104/62, heart rate 112, respiratory rate 24, temperature 98.9, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. Your breathing is deep and fast, your mouth is dry, and your belly is tender in the middle but soft, with no guarding. Your fingerstick glucose is 486. The blood tests show a venous pH of 7.18, bicarbonate 10, potassium 5.4, sodium 131, and creatinine 1.5, and your ketones are high, with a beta-hydroxybutyrate of 5.2.
Patient: That sounds bad.
Doctor: It is serious but treatable. I think this is hyperglycemia with diabetic ketoacidosis, triggered by missing your insulin during the stomach illness, and you also have dehydration and some acute kidney injury. Here is the plan. We'll give you a liter of normal saline right now and keep the fluids going, then start an insulin infusion once we confirm your potassium is safe. I'll give ondansetron 4 mg IV for the nausea. Hold the metformin while your kidneys recover. We'll recheck your labs every 2 hours, get an ECG, and send a urinalysis and a lactate. You'll be admitted to the ICU for close monitoring.
Patient: Okay. Will I be there long?
Doctor: Probably a day or two. Once the acid clears, we'll restart your long-acting insulin, and I want you to know never to stop your basal insulin when you're sick, even if you can't eat.
summary: A 60-year-old male with diabetes presented to the emergency department after three days of a stomach illness with vomiting, during which he skipped his insulin glargine for two nights. He reported intense thirst, frequent urination, abdominal pain, weakness and fast breathing, and denied fever, chest pain, cough and diarrhea. He was tachycardic and tachypneic with a glucose of 486, venous pH 7.18, potassium 5.4 and creatinine 1.5. The clinician diagnosed hyperglycemia with diabetic ketoacidosis, dehydration and acute kidney injury. He will receive normal saline, an insulin infusion and ondansetron, metformin is held, and he is admitted to the ICU.

soap.subjective: Sick for about three days with a stomach bug and vomiting, unable to keep food down, so he stopped his insulin; he skipped insulin glargine for two nights. Now very thirsty, urinating frequently, with stomach pain, weakness and fast breathing. Denies fever, chest pain, cough and diarrhea. Takes insulin glargine 30 units at night and metformin 1000 mg twice a day. Has diabetes.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 104/62, heart rate 112, respiratory rate 24, temperature 98.9, oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. Deep and fast breathing, dry mouth, belly tender in the middle but soft with no guarding. Fingerstick glucose 486. Venous pH 7.18, bicarbonate 10, potassium 5.4, sodium 131, creatinine 1.5, beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.2 with high ketones.
soap.assessment: Hyperglycemia with diabetic ketoacidosis triggered by missed insulin during a stomach illness, with dehydration and acute kidney injury.
plan: Normal saline 1 liter now and continue fluids
Start an insulin infusion once potassium is confirmed safe
Ondansetron 4 mg IV for nausea
Hold metformin while kidneys recover

Restart long-acting insulin once the acid clears and never stop basal insulin when sick

note:
Gastroenterology clinic follow-up for a 72-year-old female referred by her primary care physician for progressive dysphagia.

History: She reports difficulty swallowing solid foods that began about 4 months ago and has progressed from occasional trouble with bread and meat to difficulty with most solids. Food sticks at the lower breastbone, and she sometimes regurgitates undigested food shortly after swallowing. She can still drink liquids without trouble. She has lost about 10 pounds over 4 months. She also describes pills sticking in her chest. She denies odynophagia, hematemesis, melena, hoarseness, cough with meals, and chest pain. She has never had esophageal dilation or surgery.

Past history includes atrial fibrillation, HTN, T2DM, GERD for many years, hypothyroidism, and osteoporosis. She has no known drug allergies.

Medications: She first stated that she takes apixaban 5 mg once daily. Her daughter, who fills her weekly pillbox, clarified, and the pharmacy list confirms, that she takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily; correction, the dose is 5 mg twice daily, not once daily. She also takes omeprazole 20 mg daily, alendronate 70 mg weekly, amlodipine 5 mg daily, levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, and metformin 500 mg twice daily. Her over-the-counter supplements include fish oil 1000 mg daily, turmeric capsules, and calcium carbonate with vitamin D.

Vitals today: BP 134/78, HR 72, temperature 98.0 F. Weight is 132 pounds, down from 142 pounds 4 months ago. She has mild conjunctival pallor. She is thin and in no distress. There is no supraclavicular adenopathy, the abdomen is soft and nontender, and there is no hepatomegaly.

Data: Barium esophagram last week showed a smooth tapered narrowing of the distal esophagus about 3 cm in length with mild proximal dilation and delayed passage of a 13 mm tablet. Labs 2 weeks ago showed Hgb 11.2, MCV 78, ferritin 14, creatinine 1.1, eGFR 58, and A1c 6.9%.

Impression: Progressive solid-food dysphagia with weight loss and iron deficiency anemia, most consistent with a distal esophageal stricture, likely peptic from long-standing GERD, with possible contribution from alendronate. Malignancy must be excluded.

Recommendations: Schedule EGD with biopsies and possible dilation within 1 week under monitored anesthesia care. Hold apixaban for 2 days before the EGD, no bridging is needed, and resume 24 hours afterward if there is no bleeding. Stop fish oil and turmeric capsules 7 days before the procedure. Discontinue alendronate, and her primary care physician will arrange a different osteoporosis therapy. Increase omeprazole from 20 mg daily to 40 mg daily, taken 30 minutes before breakfast. Advise a soft diet with small bites, sitting upright for meals, and taking pills with a full glass of water. Recheck CBC and ferritin at the post-procedure visit, since iron replacement is deferred until after the EGD. Return to the emergency department for inability to swallow saliva, food stuck in the chest, vomiting blood, or black stools. Clinic follow-up after the EGD to review the biopsy results.

Plan includes EGD with biopsies and possible dilation, holding apixaban and supplements beforehand, stopping alendronate, and increasing omeprazole to 40 mg daily.

Hospital day 2 for a 54-year-old female admitted with palpitations. She describes a racing, irregular heartbeat that started the evening before admission and lasted several hours, along with fatigue. She denies chest pain, syncope, lightheadedness, and shortness of breath. On admission telemetry showed atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 110 to 140, which converted spontaneously to sinus rhythm in the early morning of hospital day 1. Since then she has remained in sinus rhythm with rates in the 60s and 70s and had no further palpitations overnight.

Her history includes HTN and known paroxysmal atrial fibrillation diagnosed last year. On direct questioning she admitted that she has been taking her metoprolol succinate 50 mg only every other day for the past few months because of cost, and that she stopped apixaban 3 months ago because the copay was too high. She continues to take lisinopril 20 mg daily, which is a low-cost generic.

Vitals this morning are BP 126/74, HR 68, RR 16, temperature 98.2 F, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Heart is regular without murmur, lungs are clear, and there is no peripheral edema. Admission potassium was 3.4 and was replaced with potassium chloride 40 mEq by mouth, and this morning it is 4.0. Magnesium is 1.9. Troponin was negative twice, TSH is 1.9, hemoglobin is 13.1, and creatinine is 0.8. ECG this morning shows sinus rhythm. Echocardiogram showed an ejection fraction of 60%, mild left atrial enlargement, and no significant valve disease.

Impression is paroxysmal atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular rate, likely triggered by hypokalemia and by inconsistent beta-blocker use because of medication costs. Her stroke risk score is 2 from female sex and HTN, so anticoagulation is indicated.

Plan: Restart apixaban 5 mg twice daily. Change metoprolol succinate to the low-cost generic metoprolol tartrate 25 mg twice daily. Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily. Case management and pharmacy have been asked to enroll her in a medication assistance program and to review a monthly cost estimate before discharge; if apixaban remains unaffordable, warfarin with INR monitoring is the alternative. We discussed that skipping doses can cause her atrial fibrillation to recur and raises her stroke risk. Continue telemetry, anticipate discharge tomorrow if she stays in sinus rhythm, repeat BMP in 1 week, and cardiology clinic follow-up in 2 weeks.

Troponin was negative twice, TSH and echocardiogram were unremarkable apart from mild left atrial enlargement, and admission potassium of 3.4 was replaced. Plan is to restart apixaban 5 mg twice daily, switch to metoprolol tartrate 25 mg twice daily, enroll her in a medication assistance program, repeat a BMP in 1 week and arrange cardiology follow-up.

Doctor: Welcome back. This is your three-month visit, and I see in the chart that you're a 31-year-old female living with HIV, on your current treatment for about two years. How have you been?
Patient: Honestly, a little anxious. I read online that HIV pills can damage your kidneys and liver, and I keep worrying about it. Is that going to happen to me? And what if the virus becomes resistant? Also, I've had some headaches. Is that from the medicine?
Doctor: Those are good questions and I'll go through each one. First, are you still taking Biktarvy, one tablet once daily?
Patient: Yes, every morning with breakfast. I haven't missed a single dose.
Doctor: Wonderful. Your labs from last week look excellent. Your viral load is undetectable, less than 20 copies, your CD4 count is 640, creatinine is 0.8, eGFR is 105, and your liver tests are normal. So your kidneys and liver are fine and the virus is well controlled.
Patient: So the pills aren't hurting me? What about resistance if I miss one?
Doctor: An occasional missed dose is unlikely to cause trouble with this regimen, but taking it every day is the best protection. About the headaches, how often do you get them?
Patient: Maybe twice a week, mild, usually in the afternoon. And I've had trouble sleeping because I keep worrying. No fever, no night sweats, no weight loss, no diarrhea, and no rash.
Doctor: Thank you. Your blood pressure today is 118/72, heart rate 80, and temperature 98.4. Your lymph nodes feel normal, your mouth is clear with no thrush, and your lungs are clear.
Patient: One more thing. My partner and I want to have a baby next year. Is that possible? Could I pass HIV to the baby, or to my partner?
Doctor: Yes, it is possible. With an undetectable viral load there is essentially no risk of sexual transmission to your partner, and the risk to the baby is very low if you keep taking treatment. Since you're planning a pregnancy, I'd like you to start folic acid 0.4 mg daily now. We can keep your current regimen.
Patient: Okay. Do I need any tests?
Doctor: It's been three years since your last Pap smear, so we'll do a Pap smear today, send urine testing for gonorrhea and chlamydia, and give you your flu shot.
Patient: And the anxious feelings?
Doctor: Anxiety is very understandable, and your headaches are probably related to stress and poor sleep rather than the medicine. Try limiting caffeine in the afternoon, and I'll refer you to our clinic counselor. If it persists we can talk about medication. Continue Biktarvy one tablet once daily, and come back in three months for a repeat viral load, or sooner if you have any concerns.
Patient: Thank you, that helps a lot.
summary: A 31-year-old female with HIV on antiretroviral therapy for about two years presented for routine follow-up, feeling anxious and asking about drug toxicity, resistance, headaches and pregnancy planning. She reports mild headaches and trouble sleeping, takes Biktarvy daily without missed doses, and denies fever, night sweats, weight loss, diarrhea and rash. Labs showed an undetectable viral load, CD4 count 640, creatinine 0.8 and eGFR 105. The clinician reassured her and attributed the headaches to stress and poor sleep. Plan is to continue Biktarvy, start folic acid 0.4 mg daily, do a Pap smear and urine testing, give a flu shot, refer to a counselor, and see her in three months.

Doctor: Hello, I'm the emergency physician. A professional Vietnamese interpreter is with us on the video screen, so please speak in your own language and the interpreter will translate. I have you down as a 56-year-old female with diabetes. What brought you in?
Interpreter: The patient says she has been very thirsty and urinating a lot for three days, and for the last day she has been vomiting and has pain in the upper belly.
Patient: And I feel very tired, and my breathing is fast.
Doctor: Does it hurt when you urinate? Any fever, chest pain, or diarrhea?
Interpreter: She says yes, it burned when she urinated starting about a week ago. But no fever, no chest pain, and no diarrhea.
Doctor: Which diabetes medicines do you take?
Interpreter: She takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily, and a new pill her family doctor started three weeks ago called empagliflozin, 25 mg once daily.
Doctor: Any insulin?
Interpreter: No insulin.
Doctor: Okay, thank you. Your blood pressure is 98/58, heart rate 118, respiratory rate 26, temperature 99.1, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. Your mouth is dry, your breathing is deep and rapid, and your upper belly is tender without guarding. Your fingerstick glucose is 388. The blood tests show a venous pH of 7.12, bicarbonate 9, sodium 134, potassium 4.9, and creatinine 1.6, and there are large ketones in the urine. The urine also shows white cells and nitrites, which means a urinary infection.
Interpreter: The patient asks if this is dangerous.
Doctor: Yes, it is serious. Please tell her I believe she has diabetic ketoacidosis, which can happen with empagliflozin even when the sugar is not extremely high, along with a urinary tract infection and dehydration. Here is the plan. I am stopping the empagliflozin and holding the metformin because of her kidney numbers. We will give 1 liter of normal saline now and continue fluids, start an insulin infusion after rechecking her potassium, give ceftriaxone 1 gram IV for the urinary infection, and send blood and urine cultures. We will repeat blood tests every 2 hours, and she will be admitted to the ICU.
Interpreter: I have explained everything. She understands and agrees. She asks if someone can call her daughter.
Doctor: Yes, we will call her daughter once she is settled in the ICU.
summary: A 56-year-old female with diabetes was seen in the emergency department with a professional Vietnamese interpreter for three days of thirst and frequent urination, a day of vomiting and upper abdominal pain, fatigue, fast breathing, and burning with urination for a week. She denies fever, chest pain and diarrhea, and empagliflozin was started three weeks ago. She was hypotensive and tachycardic with a glucose of 388, venous pH 7.12, creatinine 1.6 and large urine ketones with white cells and nitrites. The clinician diagnosed diabetic ketoacidosis with a urinary tract infection and dehydration. Empagliflozin is stopped, metformin held, and she receives normal saline, an insulin infusion and ceftriaxone with ICU admission.

note: This is a dictation for a pulmonology follow-up visit on an 81-year-old female with obstructive sleep apnea on CPAP. She was diagnosed 16 months ago, correction, 14 months ago, with an AHI of 32 on her diagnostic study and has used an auto CPAP with a pressure range of 6 to 14 centimeters of water ever since. History of present illness, her main complaint today is that she does not like the mask. She says the air leaks around her full face mask, she has dry mouth, and she wakes up bloated from swallowing air so she often takes the mask off in the middle of the night. She still feels sleepy in the afternoon. She denies morning headaches, denies choking or gasping at night, denies falling asleep while talking or eating, and denies chest pain. Her Epworth score today is 11. Past history includes hypertension and hypothyroidism. Medications are amlodipine 5 mg daily, levothyroxine 50 mcg daily, and zolpidem 5 mg at bedtime, which her primary doctor started for insomnia 6 months ago. No known drug allergies. The CPAP download for the last 30 days shows use on 21 of 30 nights, average use 3.8 hours per night, use longer than 4 hours on only 38 percent of nights, a residual AHI of 4.1, and a 95th percentile leak of 38 liters per minute, which is high. Vitals today are blood pressure 136/78, pulse 70, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, BMI 31, and neck circumference 16 inches. On exam she is comfortable, Mallampati class 3, and lungs are clear. There is no leg edema. She has mild nasal congestion with pale turbinates. Assessment and plan, obstructive sleep apnea with suboptimal CPAP adherence because of mask leak, dry mouth, and aerophagia, and her residual events are low when she does wear it. Plan one, mask refit through her DME supplier with a different size full face mask and a chin strap. Plan two, increase the heated humidifier setting from 2 to 4. Plan three, change the auto CPAP range to 6 to 12 centimeters of water to reduce air swallowing. Plan four, start fluticasone nasal spray 50 mcg, one spray in each nostril once daily for the congestion. Plan five, stop zolpidem 5 mg because it can worsen sleep apnea and raises her fall risk at her age, and I will notify her primary doctor and recommend cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia. Repeat CPAP download in 6 weeks and return to clinic in 3 months. End of dictation.

Doctor: Good morning. You're a 59-year-old female with breast cancer, ten days out from cycle 2 of docetaxel and cyclophosphamide, here for your nadir blood count check. How are you feeling?
Patient: Tired, mostly. I've been wiped out since last weekend. And my mouth felt a little sore, but it's not terrible.
Doctor: Any fever, chills, sore throat, or cough?
Patient: No fever, I check it twice a day, and it was 98.2 this morning. No chills, no sore throat, no cough.
Doctor: Any burning when you pee, diarrhea, or redness at your port?
Patient: No, none of those. And no bone pain either.
Doctor: Which medicines are you taking right now?
Patient: Ondansetron 8 mg when I feel nauseated, which hasn't been much. That's all besides the chemo.
Doctor: Good. Your temperature today is 98.2, blood pressure 118/70, heart rate 84, and oxygen saturation 98 percent. Your mouth looks fine with no ulcers, the lungs are clear, and the port site is clean and dry. Your labs came back this morning. The white count is 1.8, your absolute neutrophil count is 700, hemoglobin is 10.9, and platelets are 148.
Patient: Is that bad?
Doctor: It's low, but it is the expected nadir. This is neutropenia from the chemotherapy. Because you have no fever, it is not febrile neutropenia, so you don't need to go to the hospital today and we won't change your chemo right now.
Patient: Will my next chemo be delayed?
Doctor: We'll decide based on your count on the day. If the neutrophil count is under 1000, we may delay by a week. To prevent this next time, starting with cycle 3 you'll get pegfilgrastim 6 mg as an injection 24 hours after chemo. Take loratadine 10 mg daily for 5 days starting the day of the injection to prevent bone pain. We'll repeat a CBC in 1 week and again before cycle 3.
Patient: What should I watch for?
Doctor: Check your temperature twice a day, and call us right away for 100.4 or higher, chills, sore throat, or burning with urination. Don't take acetaminophen before checking your temperature. Wash your hands often, avoid sick contacts, and skip raw or undercooked foods. If you get a fever, go straight to the emergency department.
Patient: Okay, I understand.
summary: A 59-year-old female with breast cancer, ten days after cycle 2 of docetaxel and cyclophosphamide, presented for a nadir blood count check with fatigue and a mildly sore mouth. She denies fever, chills, sore throat, cough, burning with urination, diarrhea, port redness and bone pain, and she is afebrile at 98.2. Labs showed a white count of 1.8, an absolute neutrophil count of 700, hemoglobin 10.9 and platelets 148. The clinician diagnosed expected chemotherapy-induced neutropenia without fever. Plan is pegfilgrastim 6 mg after chemo starting with cycle 3, loratadine 10 mg daily for bone pain, repeat CBC in 1 week, neutropenic precautions, and delay of chemo if the count is low on the treatment day.
